~alea Handbook · contents

The alea guide

This guide teaches alea from the first line to works made of works. Each chapter goes with one file of the tour in examples/tour/: read the chapter, run the file, change it, run it again.

alea examples/tour/01-hello.alea            # writes the edition's files in the current folder

Or open the playground (web/dist/playground.html) and pick the tour in the example menu. For the exact rules (every parameter, default and limit) see the reference.

1. A work, and its editions

Tour: 01-hello.alea

work Hello {
  field waves = sin(x * ~between(5, 40))
  render image(waves)
}

A program in alea is a work. A work doesn't describe one picture; it describes a whole family of possible pictures. Each time you run it, alea draws one member of that family, called an edition, and renders it.

~between(5, 40) is the only uncertain part of this work: each run draws a number between 5 and 40, so each edition has a different number of stripes. Everything else is fixed.

Every edition has a seed, printed when it's made:

`Hello` — edition 0x6c76b826fc738291

The seed is the edition's identity. Give it back and you get exactly the same files, byte for byte, on any computer and in the browser:

alea examples/tour/01-hello.alea --seed 0x6c76b826fc738291

So a work is like a printing plate and a seed like a print number, except that every print is different, and any print can be made again.

The shape of a file. A file holds one work: work, a name, and between braces a list of statements. Comments start with // (or #) and run to the end of the line.

2. Shapes, and what alea decides

Tour: 02-shapes.alea

let anywhere = circle()
let placed   = square(x: 0.72, y: 0.28, size: 0.18)
let exact    = ring(x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.85, width: 0.01)

alea has a vocabulary of primitives: shapes (circle, ring, rect, square, line, blob), textures, transforms and more. The rule that matters most:

Anything you leave out, alea decides.

circle() is a circle somewhere, of some size: alea draws both. Give it x and y and the position is yours, the size still alea's. Give everything and nothing is left to chance. Precision is how you take control back.

Where things are. The canvas goes from 0 to 1 in both directions, with (0, 0) at the top-left and (1, 1) at the bottom-right. Sizes are fractions of the canvas: size: 0.5 is half its width. Angles are in degrees.

Arguments. Name them (circle(x: 0.5, size: 0.2), in any order) or give them in the order the reference lists (circle(0.5, 0.5, 0.2) is x, y, size). Unnamed ones come first.

Naming things. let name = … gives a name to a value so you can use it again, in the lines that follow. Statements run from top to bottom, so a name must be given before it's used; giving the same name again replaces it from that line on.

3. Chance

Tour: 03-chance.alea

alea has three ways to involve chance. The first is the draw.

between(0.08, 0.3) is a distribution: a value that hasn't been decided yet. On its own it isn't a number; you can name it, but you can't compute with it. ~ draws from it, which gives a number.

let spread = between(0.08, 0.3)      // a distribution
let r      = ~spread                 // a number, drawn once
let left   = circle(size: r)
let right  = circle(size: r)         // same size as `left`
let a      = circle(size: ~spread)
let b      = circle(size: ~spread)   // a different size from `a`

When is a draw made? Where the ~ is written, once:

  • in a let, once per edition. The name keeps that value everywhere it's used.
  • written twice, twice: two independent values.
  • inside a pattern's events (chapter 10), once per event.
  • inside a work's parameter default (chapter 15), once per call.
  • inside a choose branch (chapter 4), only if that branch is chosen.

The distributions.

Distribution Gives
uniform(a, b), also between(a, b) any value from a to b, all equally likely
normal(m, d), also around(m, d) values around m; about two in three fall within d of it
beta(a, b) a value from 0 to 1, leaning towards 0 when a < b, towards 1 when a > b
poisson(λ) a whole number, λ on average (good for "how many")
exponential(λ) mostly small values, occasionally large ones (average 1/λ)

The second kind of chance is the grain, ~~. Where ~ draws once, ~~ draws again at every point of the canvas (and every moment of a video):

field grain = ~~uniform(0, 1) * 0.12

A grain is still fixed by the seed: the same edition has the same grain.

The third is the choice, next.

4. Choices

Tour: 04-choices.alea

choose picks one of several branches:

let motif = choose {
    3: circle(x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.55)
  | 2: square(x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.5, angle: 45)
  | 1: blob(x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.6)
}

Branches are separated by |. The number before the colon is a weight: here the circle comes up 3 times in 6, the square 2 in 6, the blob 1 in 6. Without weights, every branch is equally likely.

A choice is structural: it doesn't nudge a number, it changes what the work is made of. Only the chosen branch is drawn at all.

A branch can give anything: a shape, a number (choose { 2 | 3 | 4 }), or a text (choose { "ink" | "sea" }, handy for palettes).

5. Combining

Tour: 05-combining.alea

Shapes are 1 inside and 0 outside, with a soft edge in between. Combining them is combining those values:

Write You get
merge(a, b, …) everything, on top of each other
overlap(a, b, …) only where they all are
cut(a, b) a, with b removed
invert(a) inside and outside swapped
a + b the values added: layers
a * 0.4 a lighter tone of a
mix(a, b, amount) a blend from a (0) to b (1)
threshold(a, level: 0.5) soft tones turned into a crisp edge

Several renders. This file has seven render image lines, and running it writes seven pictures. A work can render as many times, and in as many media, as you like. All its renders belong to the same edition.

6. Transforms

Tour: 06-transforms.alea

A transform takes a shape (or a texture, or a picture, or a whole composition) and changes where it's drawn:

Transform Effect
move(s, x: 0.1, y: 0) shifts by a distance
rotate(s, angle: 30) turns around the centre (or around x, y)
zoom(s, by: 2) scales; 2 is twice as big, 0.5 half
tile(s, count: 3) repeats the whole canvas in a 3 × 3 grid
mirror(s, axis: "both") adds the reflection across the centre line(s)
kaleidoscope(s, sides: 6) repeats what lies to the right of the centre, all around it
warp(s, amount: 0.05) bends everything, like a hand-drawn line

Transforms nest, and read from the inside out:

rotate(kaleidoscope(warp(leaf, amount: 0.05), sides: 5), angle: 18)

warps the leaf, folds it into a five-petal flower, then turns the flower.

Like every primitive, a transform decides what you leave out: rotate(shape) picks an angle; kaleidoscope(shape) picks how many sides.

Watch out: this includes the parameter you didn't think of. move(shape, x: 0.01) moves right by 0.01 and up or down by a random amount, because y was left to alea. When you need an exact transform (for example to compare a field with a slightly shifted copy of itself), give every parameter: move(shape, x: 0.01, y: 0).

7. Textures

Tour: 07-textures.alea

Textures fill the whole canvas with values from 0 to 1: stripes, waves, ripples, dots, checker, gradient, glow, clouds, grain, and scatter (random specks). Most have a softness from 0 (sharp) to 1 (smooth). They combine with shapes like anything else: stripes seen through a circle is overlap(stripes(), circle()).

8. Words and pictures

Tour: 08-words-and-pictures.alea

let word  = text("alea", x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.3, font: "bold")
let photo = picture("../assets/astronaut.png")

text draws a line of text as a shape; size is the height of the line. Fonts: "sans" (default), "bold", "serif", "mono", or the path to any .ttf / .otf file.

picture brings in a PNG, JPEG or WebP image, as a field of its brightness. By default it fills the canvas width, centred. channel: "alpha" uses a transparent PNG's transparency instead, which turns a logo or a cut-out into a shape. Paths are relative to the .alea file.

These two are the exception to "alea decides": they show your content, so by default text is level and a picture fills the width.

Both are shapes: warp(text(…)), kaleidoscope(picture(…)), overlap(photo, text("SPACE")) (the photo seen through the letters).

9. Fields: the maths underneath

Tour: 09-fields.alea

Underneath every shape is a field: a number at every point (x, y) of the canvas, and every moment t. x and y are themselves fields:

field across = x                                   // 0 on the left, 1 on the right
field centre = distance(x, y, 0.5, 0.5)            // 0 in the middle
field rings  = sin(centre * 60)
field marble = sin(x * 12 + 4 * noise(x * 4, y * 4, 0))

Arithmetic (+ - * / % ^) and functions (sin, abs, noise, smoothstep…) build new fields from old ones. A comparison gives 1 where it's true and 0 where it's false, so (x > 0.5) * rings is rings on the right half only.

field name = … is like let, but insists the value is a field (not a text or a distribution), which catches mistakes early.

You never have to write maths: every primitive is a field built this way. But the two mix freely, so circle() * marble is a marbled disc.

10. Patterns: many of something

Tour: 10-patterns.alea

pattern rain = repeat 300 event(
    x: ~uniform(0, 1),
    y: ~beta(5, 2),
    intensity: ~between(0.3, 1),
    size: ~between(0.002, 0.01)
)

A pattern is a set of events. repeat N event(…) makes N of them, and every ~ inside is drawn again for each event, so the 300 drops differ. An event has five attributes; what you leave out is drawn at random:

Attribute Meaning If omitted
x, y where anywhere
t when (0 to 1) any time
intensity how strong 1
size how big (the spread of its spot) 0.02

Inside an event, i is the event's number (0, 1, 2, …) and n is how many there are, so i / n goes from 0 to almost 1: use them for order, spirals and sequences.

A pattern used as a field shows each event as a soft spot. In a sound, its events become notes (chapter 13). scatter(count, size) is a ready-made pattern of random specks.

11. Constraints: what must be true

Tour: 11-constraints.alea

constraint maximum(overlap(a, b)) < 0.5      // the circles never touch
constraint count(stars) >= 35 and count(stars) <= 45

A constraint is a condition every edition must meet. When one fails, alea throws the whole edition away and draws it again (up to 1000 times). You state the goal; chance finds a way to reach it.

To write conditions about whole fields, alea measures them over the canvas: mean, stddev (how varied), minimum, maximum. count(pattern) gives the number of events. Conditions combine with and and or.

If no edition can satisfy the constraints, alea says which one kept failing. When an edition needed several tries, it says so:

`Constraints` — edition 0x000000000000002a — 3 attempts to satisfy the constraints

12. Time: works that move

Tour: 12-time-and-video.alea

t is time. In an image it's 0 (or the render's at); over a video or a sound, it goes from 0 at the start to 1 at the end.

let beat  = lfo()                             // 0 → 1 → 0 over the video
let heart = circle(x: 0.5, y: 0.5, size: 0.15 + 0.2 * beat)
let spin  = rotate(stripes(), angle: t * 180)

Any parameter can use t. lfo() goes from 0 up to 1 and back to where it started, so motion built on it loops without a jump; lfo(3) does it three times. It is 0.5 - 0.5 * cos(t * tau) (tau is a full turn, 2π), which you can still write yourself. Chapter 21 has more ways to move.

render video(piece, duration: 4) writes an MP4 (with a soundtrack: see the next chapter) using ffmpeg; format: "gif" writes a silent loop. render image(piece, at: 0.5) takes a still from the middle.

13. Sound: layers of listening

Tour: 13-sound.alea

A soundtrack is made of layers, each listening to the work in its own way:

render sound(drone(sky, instrument: "strings", scale: "dorian", key: 110),
             notes(bells, instrument: "marimba", scale: "dorian", key: 220, tempo: 100),
             texture(mist, kind: "wind"),
             duration: 12, room: 0.5, echo: 0.2)
  • drone(field): voices that hold notes of a scale. Each listens to the field along one row of the canvas (the top row sounds lowest): loud where the field is high, brighter when louder, and on the left or the right where the field is higher on that side.
  • notes(pattern): each event plays a note. Its t is when (on the beat if you give a tempo), its y which note of the scale (higher on the canvas, higher in pitch), its x where it sounds, its size how long it rings, its intensity how loud.
  • texture(field): an ambience ("wind", "waves", "rain", "crackle") that grows louder as more of the field lights up.

Each layer has an instrument (strings, choir, organ, glass…; for notes: bell, pluck, marimba, kalimba, drum…), a scale (major, minor, dorian, pentatonic, blues…), a key in hertz and a gain. Around the mix, room gives a space (0 none, 0.9 a cathedral) and echo a repeat between left and right.

A layer can listen to anything, not only what's on screen: the drone of a video can follow the sky while the picture shows the sea. In a video, give the layers to sound::

render video(piece, duration: 20, sound: [drone(sky), notes(rain)], room: 0.6)

Without layers, render sound(field, pattern) makes the original sound: a sine drone and bell notes, in mono.

14. Sculpture

Tour: 14-sculpture.alea

render sculpture(field) turns values into heights: low values are the floor, high values the peaks, on a solid base. The result is an STL file, the format 3D-printing software reads, measured in millimetres. side is the width, base the thickness of the base, relief the height of the tallest point as a fraction of the side, and resolution how fine the surface is.

15. Works made of works

Tour: 15-components.alea and lib/flower.alea

A work can be used inside another. Give it parameters and an output:

work Flower(cx = ~between(0.2, 0.8), cy = ~between(0.2, 0.8),
            size = ~between(0.12, 0.22), petals = choose { 5 | 6 | 8 }) {
  let petal = blob(x: cx + size * 0.55, y: cy, size: size * 0.7)
  output kaleidoscope(petal, sides: petals, x: cx, y: cy)
  render image(output)          // only when this file runs on its own
}

and bring it in with use:

use "lib/flower.alea"

work Garden {
  let a = Flower()                                   // a new draw
  let b = Flower()                                   // another one
  let centre = Flower(cx: 0.5, cy: 0.5, petals: 12)  // some decisions taken back
  render image(merge(a, b, centre))
}

The rules:

  • Every call is a new draw. Flower() twice is two different flowers. To use one flower twice, bind it: let f = Flower().
  • Parameters work like a primitive's: a caller gives some, the defaults draw the rest. A parameter without a default must be given (work Frame(art, margin = 0.08)), and a parameter can be a shape, which makes a work a reusable effect.
  • One seed still replays everything, components included. Each instance keeps its own grain and noise.
  • Constraints stay local: a component that fails its own constraint is redrawn on its own, without redrawing the piece around it.
  • A component's renders are ignored when it's used; only output counts. The same file is a standalone piece and a component.
  • x, y, t can't be parameter names, since they mean the canvas and time: call a centre cx, cy.

16. Everything together

Tour: 16-lighthouse.alea

The last file draws a horizon at a random height, a sky of clouds and a number of stars that a constraint keeps above 110, a sea of warped waves, and a lighthouse whose beam turns once over the video. It renders an image, a video and a sound from the same edition.

17. Growing: fields with a memory

Tour: 17-life.alea

Everything so far is a function of the place and the moment: alea can compute any point of any frame on its own. Some things can't be described that way. In Conway's Game of Life, whether a cell is alive depends on its neighbours one generation earlier, and theirs on the generation before. For that, a field has to remember. That is what grow does:

grow over 160 for 360 {
  cells = ~~uniform(0, 1) < 0.3
    then neighbours(cells) == 3 or (cells and neighbours(cells) == 2)
}
  • over 160: the canvas is a grid of 160 × 160 cells. for 360: there are 360 generations after the first.
  • Each line reads name = start then next. start is generation 0. next computes the following generation; inside it, cells means the previous generation.
  • Inside next, three helpers look at the cells around each cell:
  • neighbours(f): the sum of the 8 cells around it;
  • spread(f): how much the surroundings exceed the cell itself (a diffusion: add it, and the field spreads out evenly);
  • nearby(f, r): the average over a disc of r cells.
  • After the block, cells is an ordinary field. t runs through the generations, from the first (t = 0) to the last (t = 1), and between cells and between generations the values are blended smoothly. The grid wraps around: what leaves on the right comes back on the left.

Several lines in one block grow together: each next sees the previous generation of all of them. That's how two chemicals react and spread (a reaction–diffusion, the maths behind spots, stripes and corals):

grow over 256 for 6000 {
  food = 1 - 0.5 * seeds
    then food + spread(food) - food * life * life + 0.055 * (1 - food)
  life = 0.25 * seeds
    then life + 0.5 * spread(life) + food * life * life - 0.117 * life
}

Chance still works the usual way. ~ in a rule is drawn once, ~~ gives each cell its own draw (and a new one at each generation). Inside next, t is the generation's moment, so a rule can change over time.

Growing takes time: it is computed when the edition is drawn, cell by cell, generation by generation, before anything is rendered. A grid of 128 cells for a few hundred generations is instant; 256 cells for thousands of generations takes a minute or two.

18. Lists and functions

Tour: 18-lists.alea

A list holds several values: [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]. A point is a list of two numbers, [x, y], and .x and .y read them. list[0] is the first element, list[-1] the last; count(list) says how many there are.

let stops = [[0.1, 0.8], [0.4, 0.3], [0.9, 0.5]]
let first = stops[0]
let tip = circle(first.x, first.y, 0.05)

A loop builds a list, one element for each element of another. range(n) counts from 0 to n − 1:

let dots  = [circle(p.x, p.y, 0.03) for p in stops]     // one circle per stop
let bars  = [rect(0.1 + k * 0.1, 0.5, 0.05, 0.6) for k in range(8)]
let grid  = [[a / 4, b / 4] for a in range(5) for b in range(5)]   // two loops: 25 points

Each ~ in a loop is drawn again for every element: [~between(0, 1) for k in range(10)] is ten different numbers.

Putting a list together. merge(list) draws everything in it, overlap(list) keeps only where all of it is. sum, mean, minimum, maximum work on lists of numbers or fields. join(a, b) puts lists end to end, slice(list, 1, -1) takes a part, reverse(list) turns it round.

Arithmetic works element by element, so points add, scale and blend like numbers: p + [0.1, 0] moves a point, (a + b) * 0.5 is halfway between two, and so is mix(a, b, 0.5). distance(a, b) is the distance between two points.

Paths. A list of points is also a line to draw and a road to follow:
path(points, width, softness) the line through all the points, with round joints
length(points) how long that line is
along(points, d) the point at distance d from the start (t * length(points) travels it once over the video)

A function names a calculation you use more than once:

let snap(v) = floor(v * 24 + 0.5) / 24
let star(x0, y0) = [x0 + ~around(0, 0.04), y0 + ~around(0, 0.04)]
let a = star(0.3, 0.4)      // a new draw at every call

A function's body is one expression. It sees the names given before it (not the ones after, and not itself), and its parameters can have defaults: let shade(v, k = 0.5) = v * k.

Values in texts. Inside a text, {…} puts a value: "{h} h", and "{h:02}:00" pads it with zeros to two digits, which writes 08:00.

19. Paintings: mosaics and overlays

Tour: 19-paintings.alea

A field is numbers; a render turns them into colours with one palette, over the range the field takes. Put two works in one field and they share that palette and that range. To keep each work as itself, paint it:

let map  = paint(Isohypses(), palette: "ink")
let city = paint(Correspondances(), palette: "sea")

A painting is a field in colour, with its own palette and its own range (range: [0, 1] fixes it instead of measuring it), and transparent where its alpha field is 0. Paintings are laid out and stacked:

  • mosaic(paintings, columns, gap, background): a wall of screens. Each cell shows a whole painting (its unit square, centred), side by side, each running at the same moment in a video.
  • place(painting, x, y, width, height): one painting anywhere on the canvas, at any size: a picture in a picture.
  • overlay(below, above, …, blend, opacity, mask): one painting over another. blend is "normal", "add", "screen", "multiply", "lighten", "darken", "difference" or "overlay"; opacity how much shows; mask a field saying where. To give layers different blends, put an overlay inside another.

render image and render video show a painting in its own colours (so they take no palette). A work can give a painting as its output, and then keeps its colours wherever it is used. A painting can't go into arithmetic any more: it is the end of the line, made to be seen.

let wall = mosaic([paint(Isohypses(), palette: "ink"), paint(Rosace(), palette: "ember")], columns: 2)
render video(overlay(wall, place(paint(Culture(), palette: "night"), x: 0.8, y: 0.8, width: 0.3)), duration: 15)

20. Colours of your own

Tour: 20-colours.alea

A field stays a number everywhere; colour is decided at the end, by the palette. Besides the five built in, a palette can be a list of colours:

let mondrian = ["#f2efe6", "#f5d000", "#d40920", "#1356a2", "#111111"]
render image(city, palette: mondrian)                          // a gradient through them
render image(city, palette: mondrian, bands: 5, range: [0, 1]) // five flat colours
  • A plain list is a gradient, spread evenly from the lowest value to the highest.
  • bands: n cuts it into n flat levels. With as many bands as colours, each colour gets an equal share of the values and nothing is blended: a field that takes the values 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1 shows exactly five colours. It works on named palettes too (palette: "ember", bands: 6 posterizes).
  • range: [0, 1] maps the values as they are, without stretching them to the range they take, so 0.25 is always the second colour.
  • Placed colours, [[0, "#fff"], [0.6, "#fff"], [0.6, "#d40920"], [1, "#111"]], sit at chosen values; two at the same value make a sharp edge (white up to 0.6, then red).

The same options work on paint(…), so each painting in a mosaic can have colours of its own.

21. Animation: when things happen

Tour: 21-animation.alea

t runs from 0 to 1 over a video, and anything can follow it. But writing "from 0.2 to 0.35, grow, overshooting a little" by hand is arithmetic. These functions say it directly:

  • progress(start, end): 0 before start, 1 after end, a straight line between. The building block: progress(0.2, 0.35) is a little clock that runs only during that stretch.
  • ease(v, kind): the same journey from 0 to 1, with a feel: "linear", "in" (starts slowly), "out" (arrives slowly), "in-out" (the default), "sine", "back" (overshoots, then settles), "elastic" (wobbles) or "bounce" (lands, bounces, lands).
  • keys([[time, value], …], ease): a value that passes through key frames. The values can be numbers, fields or points: keys([[0, [0.2, 0.7]], [0.5, [0.5, 0.2]], [1, [0.2, 0.7]]], ease: "in-out") is a point that travels and comes back.
  • sequence([a, b, c], fade): one thing after another, each holding an equal share of the time, crossfading over fade. Fields or paintings.
  • at(work, time): a field or a painting at another moment. at(Culture(), 0.3) is frozen, at(Culture(), 1 - t) runs backwards, and at(Culture(), ease(t, "out")) slows down to its end. Inside the work, time is whatever you give it, all the way down.
let pop  = ease(progress(0.2, 0.35), "back")
let halo = ring(0.5, 0.5, 0.5 * pop, 0.015, 0.01)
let ball = circle(0.12, 0.1 + 0.8 * ease(fract(t * 4), "bounce"), 0.05)
render video(sequence([paint(calm), paint(storm), paint(still)], fade: 0.15), duration: 12)

All of these take time: to follow another clock than t: fract(t * 4) repeats four times, progress(…, time: other) follows anything.

Going round. Most motion repeats, and two helpers say so:

  • lfo(times, shape, phase, from, to): a value that cycles, the "low-frequency oscillator" of synthesizers. lfo() goes from 0 to 1 and back once over the work; lfo(4) four times (keep it a whole number and the video loops). shape is "sine" (the default), "triangle", "saw" (a ramp), "square" or "pulse" (a hit at the start of each turn, fading). from and to set the range, and phase shifts it, in turns: [lfo(phase: k / 9) for k in range(9)] is nine values each a ninth out of step. cc(lfo(8), 74) sweeps a synth's filter.
  • orbit(radius, times, phase, x, y): a point [x, y] going round (0.5, 0.5) by default. times: [2, 3] turns twice across and three times down: a Lissajous figure. radius: [0.4, 0.2] makes an ellipse.
let p     = orbit(0.3, times: [2, 3])
let comet = circle(p.x, p.y, 0.04)
let ring  = [orbit(0.28, phase: k / 9) for k in range(9)]   // nine points, evenly round
let flash = lfo(16, shape: "pulse")                        // sixteen hits

22. Filters

Tour: 22-filters.alea

A filter changes how a picture is seen, not what it is. There are two moments to apply one.

On a field, before colour, so the result is still a field you can compute with:

  • blur(f, 0.01): softened over that distance (a fraction of the canvas).
  • pixelate(f, 0.02): in square cells of that size.
  • edges(f): only where the field changes, the outlines of shapes.
  • relief(f, angle: 135, depth: 10): lit from one side (the angle the light comes from, 90 above, 135 the upper left), like an engraving.
  • posterize(f, 6): in six flat levels.
  • film(f, 0.08): grain, new at every frame.
  • vignette(f, 0.5): darker towards the corners.

On a painting, after colour, as the very last step: blur, pixelate, film and vignette work on its pixels too, and two more only make sense in colour:

  • bloom(p, 0.8): light bleeding out of the bright parts.
  • chroma(p, 0.5): red and blue drifting apart towards the edges, like a cheap lens.
let night = paint(max(lights, land * 0.3), palette: "ember")
render image(vignette(film(chroma(bloom(night, 2.5), 0.8), 0.06), 0.6))

A field blur samples the field 40 times around each point, so it costs 40 times the field; a painting blur works on pixels and costs the same whatever is underneath. For a large blur on a heavy work, paint it first.

23. Input: works in a pipe

Tour: 23-input.alea

A work can read what you give it, and give back what it makes, so works chain like any command:

cat portrait.png | alea contours.alea > map.png
cat photo.jpg | alea soften.alea | alea poster.alea > print.png
alea contours.alea --in portrait.png -o .      # the same with files

In the work, input() is what came in: through the pipe, or with --in file. Give it a default, so the work also runs on its own:

let photo = input(or: "portrait.png")    // a file next to the work
let photo = input(or: clouds())          // or any value

An image becomes fields, which is how everything in alea is made:

  • photo.luma, and .red, .green, .blue, .alpha, .hue, .saturation, .lightness: one channel each, from 0 to 1. The image covers the canvas, and the canvas takes the image's size (or its proportions, if you give a width), so what comes out lines up with what went in.
  • photo.painting: the image in its own colours, for overlay, mosaic and the filters.
  • colours(photo, 6): its six main colours, darkest first. That's a palette, so a work can draw something new in someone else's colours.
  • photo.width, photo.height: its size in pixels.

Everything you know applies. blur(photo.luma, 0.01) softens it (a still picture is blurred once, on its pixels, so it costs nothing per frame), edges finds its outlines, posterize cuts it into levels, relief engraves it, warp and kaleidoscope bend it, and t animates it.

Piped out. When the output of alea isn't a terminal and no -o is given, the work's first render goes to it (and the edition's line to the error output). -o - asks for it explicitly.

Which edition. An edition is now its seed and its input: the line alea prints shows both (edition 0x… · input 9ea63049, a fingerprint of the input). --seed-from-input makes the input decide the seed, so the same picture always gives the same edition.

Inputs can also have names, for works that take several: alea duet.alea --in face=me.png --in voice=me.wav, read with input("face"). A text input gives .text, .words, .lines, and .rows (each line split on commas or spaces, numbers as numbers): data to draw with.

24. Listening: a sound as input

Tour: 24-listening.alea

A sound (a WAV file; anything else through ffmpeg) becomes time:

ffmpeg -i song.mp3 -f wav - | alea equaliser.alea -o .
  • song.level: how loud, from 0 to 1, along the sound. It's a field of t, like sin(t * tau), so it goes anywhere a number goes: circle(0.5, 0.5, 0.1 + 0.3 * song.level).
  • song.bass, song.mid, song.treble, and band(song, 200, 800) for any band of frequencies (in Hz).
  • song.pulse: 1 on each beat, fading within a fifth of a second. The simplest way to make something hit with the music.
  • song.beats: the beats as a pattern, one event per beat with its strength as intensity. Patterns can be drawn (a long exposure of every beat at once) and played: notes(song.beats, instrument: "glass") echoes the rhythm.
  • song.duration, in seconds.

A video that reads a sound lasts as long as the sound, and sound: [song] puts the sound itself in the soundtrack, as it is, alongside drones and notes. In other words: a music video, a different one for every seed.

25. MIDI: the music, for other instruments

Tour: 25-midi.alea

The layers of a soundtrack already decide notes: a notes layer strikes a note of the scale for each event, a drone holds notes that swell and fade. render midi writes those decisions as a MIDI file, for a DAW, a synthesizer, a score editor:

let music = [drone(tide, voices: 4, scale: "dorian"), notes(melody, instrument: "marimba", tempo: 96),
             cc(0.5 + 0.5 * sin(t * tau), 74)]
render sound(music, duration: 20)              // what alea plays
render midi(music, duration: 20, tempo: 96)    // the same music, note for note
  • Each layer is a track on its own channel, with a General MIDI instrument (strings, marimba, choir…), so the file sounds right anywhere.
  • notes: one note per event, at the same moment and pitch as in the sound, its strength as velocity. Drums go to channel 10: low on the canvas a kick, then snare, hats, cymbals at the top.
  • drone: each voice a held note, struck when it rises and released when it fades, and the loudness of the layer as expression (controller 11).
  • cc(field, number) turns a field (from 0 to 1) into a controller: a knob that moves on its own. 74 is often a synth's filter, 1 its modulation wheel; channel: (1–16) says which instrument hears it. A cc is silent in alea's own sound.
  • The tempo (tempo:, or the first notes layer's) sets the file's grid, so the bars line up in a DAW.

Live. The same music can be played as it is computed, to any MIDI instrument:

alea modes.alea --midi                 # on a new MIDI port called "alea"
alea modes.alea --midi-port "Minilogue" # to an existing one (alea --midi-ports lists them)
alea modes.alea --midi --loop          # a new edition every time one ends, until Ctrl-C
alea modes.alea --midi --sync          # following a DAW's MIDI clock: its tempo, start and stop
alea modes.alea --midi-port print      # the messages as text, to see them

What is played is the work's render midi, or, if it has none, the layers of its first render sound or video sound:. With --sync, the music's beats follow the DAW's tempo, a stop silences it and a start begins again; with --loop, each new edition starts on the next bar. Ctrl-C silences every note. Live MIDI needs alea built with cargo build --release --features midi (on Linux, after sudo apt install libasound2-dev).

In the playground, a render midi shows its notes as a piano roll, plays a rough preview in the page, plays to a MIDI device with Web MIDI (Chrome, Edge), and saves the .mid file.

26. Harmony and rhythm: a generative track

Tour: 26-harmony.alea

Music lives in bars, so the first thing is a meter:

let m = meter(100, bars: 8)          // 100 beats per minute, 8 bars of 4 beats
render sound(music, duration: m.length)
render midi(music, duration: m.length, tempo: m.tempo)

m.length is the duration in seconds, m.bar and m.beat the length of one bar and one beat. Keys can now be written as note names everywhere: key: "D3", "F#2", "Bb4" (A4 is 440 Hz).

Rhythms are patterns, so they go wherever patterns go (notes, arp, pictures, MIDI). Each spans the work, bar after bar (bars: a number or a meter), and y: sets the height of its events (for drums: low is a kick, then snare, hats, cymbals):

  • euclid(hits, steps): hits spread as evenly as possible over the steps of a bar. A small rule behind many of the world's rhythms: euclid(3, 8) is the tresillo, euclid(5, 8) the cinquillo, euclid(7, 16) a samba line. rotate: shifts it.
  • steps("X...x...X...x..o"): a step sequencer. X an accent, x a hit, o a soft hit, . a rest; | starts the next bar, and the bars written repeat.
  • steps(16, density: field): a random hit on each of 16 steps, more likely where the field is high (read left to right along the middle of the canvas as time runs): a visual decides the groove.

On notes, swing: 0.6 delays every second sixteenth (0.5 is straight, 0.66 a triplet feel) and humanize: 0.3 loosens moments and velocities. Both need the layer's tempo.

Harmony. chords makes a progression that spans the work:

let prog = chords("i iv V7 i", key: "A3", scale: "minor", bars: m)
let prog = chords("Am F C G7", bars: m)                       // chord names work too
let prog = chords("functional", key: "D3", scale: "dorian", bars: m, tension: 0.5)
  • Roman numerals count on the scale: upper case for major, lower case for minor, ° diminished, + augmented, 7, maj7, 9, 6, sus2, sus4, and b or # in front for borrowed chords (bVII). "i:2 iv V" gives the first chord twice the time.
  • "functional" draws the progression, one chord per bar, the way tonal music moves: home (tonic: I, vi, iii), away (subdominant: IV, ii), tension (dominant: V, vii°), and home again, with a cadence at the end of each phrase of four bars and V–I at the end. tension (0–1) asks for more dominants and sevenths; in a minor mode the dominant is often made major. Each edition gets a new progression that still sounds right.
  • prog.names lists its chords ("i", "IV", "V7"…), and prog.index is a field of time, 0 for the first chord, 1 for the second…: pictures can follow the harmony.

Layers follow it with harmony: prog: a drone's voices move to the nearest note of each new chord (voice leading, gliding), and notes play the notes of the chord of the moment (the height of an event picks among them, over three octaves). The layer's key keeps its register: key: prog.key / 4 is two octaves down, a bass.

The arpeggiator plays the chord one note at a time, on a rhythm:

arp(prog, euclid(7, 16, bars: m), mode: "updown", octaves: 2, gate: 0.6, instrument: "marimba")

mode is "up", "down", "updown", "random" or "converge" (from the outside in); octaves how far it climbs; gate how long each note is held before the next (in MIDI). It's a layer like notes: heard in alea's sound, written in render midi, played live with --midi, following a DAW with --sync. Its tempo comes from the meter of the progression.

27. Synths: instruments of your own

Tour: 27-synths.alea

Every instrument so far had a name, "marimba", "strings", and a sound someone else chose. A synth is an instrument you build yourself, from the parts a synthesizer is made of, and it goes wherever an instrument name went:

let pad = synth {
  let env = adsr(attack: 1, decay: 0.5, sustain: 0.8, release: 2)
  lowpass(saw() + saw(note.freq * 1.004), cutoff: 1200) * env
}
render sound(notes(melody, instrument: pad))     // drone and arp take it too

A synth is a few lets, then one expression: its sound. It is played once for every note, and note is that note: note.freq (its frequency in Hz), note.velocity (how hard it is played, from the event's intensity), note.gate (1 while it is held), note.time (seconds since it started) and, in a drone, note.level (how loud the field is there).

The parts:

  • Oscillators make the raw sound: sine() (pure), triangle() (soft), square() (hollow, a clarinet), saw() (bright, strings and brass), pulse(width: 0.2) (thin, nasal), noise() (breath, hats, rain). They play the note's frequency unless you give one: saw(note.freq / 2) is an octave down. Inside a synth, square is an oscillator; outside, still a shape.
  • Envelopes shape the loudness over time, from 0 to 1. adsr(attack, decay, sustain, release) follows the note: it rises, falls to the sustain level, holds while the note is held, then fades. perc(attack, release) is struck: it rises and dies away, however long the note.
  • Filters take part of the sound away: lowpass keeps what is below its cutoff (darker), highpass what is above (thinner), bandpass a band around it (a vowel, a whistle). resonance (0–1) makes the cutoff sing.
  • Effects: delay(sound, time, feedback) an echo, drive(sound, amount) saturation, chorus(sound) a swaying copy that widens it.

What makes a synth come alive is that anything can move anything. Multiply by an envelope, and the loudness follows it; give an envelope to a cutoff, and the sound opens and closes:

let snap = perc(release: 0.2)
lowpass(saw(), cutoff: 100 + 3000 * snap, resonance: 0.6)    // a bass that snaps shut

An oscillator inside another's frequency bends it: that is FM, frequency modulation, the sound of bells and electric pianos:

sine(note.freq + sine(note.freq * 3.5) * note.freq * 2 * perc(release: 0.5)) * perc(release: 2)

and a slow oscillator is an LFO: cutoff: 800 + 400 * sine(0.3) sweeps the filter once every three seconds.

Chance works here as everywhere: a ~ in a synth is drawn once per edition. saw(note.freq * ~around(1.0, 0.004)) detunes each edition's pad a little differently; choose { 1.4 | 2 | 3.5 } as an FM ratio gives each edition another bell. The same seed still gives back the same sound, sample for sample.

The built-in instruments, as synths. The folder examples/instruments/ has alea's instruments written as synths: marimba.alea, bell.alea, strings.alea, choir.alea… Each is a work whose output is a synth, with a few parameters; open one to see how it is made, change it, or use it:

use "instruments/marimba.alea"
notes(melody, instrument: Marimba(ring: 2, mallet: 0.6))

A synth's loudness already follows the event's intensity (and a drone's, its field), so note.velocity and note.level are for its timbre: a filter that opens on harder notes, a vowel that opens when louder. Envelope times are set once per synth (numbers, or ~ draws). The full list of parts and their settings is in the reference, under Synths.

28. Files: opening what the work needs

A work can open the files it needs, from its own folder: a photo, a sound, a poem, a MIDI file. open reads one and recognises it by its contents; what you get is the same as an input, with the same .luma, .level or .lines.

let poem  = open("poem.txt")
let photo = open("photos/harbour.jpg")

files lists a folder, and choose(list) picks one element by chance, so each edition can take its own:

let poem = open(choose(files("poems/*.txt")))   // a poem drawn for each edition

The list is in order of name, the same on every computer, so an edition picks the same file wherever it is drawn again. choose(list) is a draw like choose { … }: one in the order of the work's draws.

MIDI files. A .mid file opens as notes. song.notes is a pattern: one event per note, along the work in time, up the canvas in pitch. You can draw it, and you can play it: a note from a MIDI file keeps its pitch and its length, so notes(song.notes, instrument: …) plays the piece as written, with alea's instruments or with your own synths.

let song = open("tune.mid")
let score = zoom(song.notes, by: 0.55, x: 0.5, y: 0.95)
render sound([notes(song.tracks[0], instrument: "kalimba"),
              notes(song.tracks[1], instrument: "pluck")], duration: song.duration)

song.tracks gives each track's notes apart, song.tempo and song.duration the file's tempo and length, and song.level a curve of how much is sounding, to move a picture with the music. Compose in your DAW, export the MIDI, and let alea draw and orchestrate it.

Where files can be. In the work's folder, or in folders inside it: never an absolute path, never ... A work and its files stay together, and a web page made with --web carries them.

How values become media

Every medium receives the same thing, a field, and translates it:

Medium The field's value becomes
image, video a colour from the palette
sound the loudness of each voice over time
sculpture a height

Values are stretched to the range they actually take in this render (a few extreme points at either end are ignored, so one bright spot doesn't wash out the rest). The absolute values don't matter much; their differences do. circle() * 10 looks like circle(); circle() + stripes() * 0.1 shows the stripes faintly.

Palettes run from the lowest value to the highest (chapter 20 shows how to make your own). ink is printing: paper for low values, ink for high ones, so shapes (which are 1) come out dark. The others (sea, ember, lichen, night) run from dark to light, so shapes come out bright. That's also why a photo looks like a negative in ink: wrap it in invert(…).

Tips

  • Start from "alea decides" and take control step by step. circle() first, then give it a position once you know where you want it.
  • Bind what you want to share. A palette chosen once with let colours = choose { … } and given to every render keeps the image and the video in agreement.
  • Use a seed while you work, so you're comparing like with like: --seed 0x2a. In the playground, Live mode does this for you.
  • Make several editions to see the range of a work: alea work.alea -n 12.
  • Read the errors. They point at the line and say what was expected:

error: `circle` has no parameter `radius` — it has: x, y, size, softness --> work.alea:2:26

alea reference

The complete rules of the language: syntax, statements, values, every primitive, function and render, the command line and the limits. To learn the language, start with the guide.

Contents: Files · Lexical rules · Grammar · Statements · Expressions · Values · Chance · Primitives · Functions · Lists · Your own functions · Patterns · Growing · Paintings · Renders · Components · Command line · Limits · Reproducibility

Files

A source file has the extension .alea, is UTF-8 text, and holds exactly one work, optionally preceded by use lines:

use "other.alea"          // zero or more

work Name(param = default) {
  statement
  statement
}

Nothing may follow the closing brace. Paths in use, picture and font are relative to the folder of the file that contains them.

Lexical rules

Comments start with // or # and run to the end of the line.

Whitespace and newlines separate tokens and are otherwise ignored, with one exception: in a call, the ( must be on the same line as the name.

Names start with a letter (any alphabet) or _, and continue with letters, digits or _: petal, étoile, size_2. Case matters; by convention works are capitalized (Moon) and everything else is lowercase.

Numbers are decimal: 3, 0.25, 1_000 (underscores are ignored). A decimal point needs a digit on both sides (0.5, not .5). There is no exponent notation. Negative numbers are written with the minus operator: -2.

Texts are written between double quotes on one line: "ember". They have no escape sequences and can't contain a double quote. {expr} inside a text puts a value there (a fixed number, or a text); {expr:02} pads a whole number with zeros to that many digits: "{h:02}:00" with h = 8 is 08:00. Other numbers are written with up to six decimals.

Keywords (reserved, can't be used as names):

use  work  let  field  pattern  constraint  render  output
repeat  event  choose  and  or  grow  then

Built-in names (can't be given to a let, field, pattern or parameter):

Name Meaning
x, y the position on the canvas, 0 to 1, from the top-left
t time, 0 to 1 over a video or a sound; 0 (or at) in an image
i, n inside a pattern's event: the event's index (0 to n − 1) and the number of events
pi, tau π and 2π

output is a keyword, but after an output statement it can also be read as a value (render image(output)). for and in (in a list loop), and over and for (after grow), are only special in those places.

Symbols: { } ( ) [ ] , . : = + - * / % ^ < > <= >= == != ~ ~~ |

Grammar

program     = { "use" STRING } "work" NAME [ params ] "{" { statement } "}" ;
params      = "(" [ param { "," param } [ "," ] ] ")" ;
param       = NAME [ "=" expr ] ;

statement   = "let" NAME "=" expr
            | "let" NAME params "=" expr                      (* a function *)
            | "field" NAME "=" expr
            | "pattern" NAME "=" "repeat" expr "event" "(" [ args ] ")"
            | "constraint" expr
            | "render" NAME "(" [ args ] ")"
            | "output" expr
            | "grow" [ "over" expr ] [ "for" expr ] "{" { NAME "=" expr "then" expr } "}" ;

args        = arg { "," arg } [ "," ] ;
arg         = [ NAME ":" ] expr ;

expr        = expr binop expr | unop expr | postfix ;
postfix     = primary { "[" expr "]" | "." NAME } ;
binop       = "or" | "and" | "<" | ">" | "<=" | ">=" | "==" | "!="
            | "+" | "-" | "*" | "/" | "%" | "^" ;
unop        = "-" | "~" | "~~" ;
primary     = NUMBER | STRING | NAME
            | NAME "(" [ args ] ")"
            | "(" expr ")"
            | "choose" "{" branch { "|" branch } "}"
            | "[" [ expr { "," expr } [ "," ] ] "]"
            | "[" expr ( "for" NAME "in" expr )+ "]" ;
branch      = [ expr ":" ] expr ;

In an argument list, unnamed arguments must come before named ones. In list[i], the [ must be on the same line as what it indexes.

Statements

Statements run from top to bottom. A name can only be used after the statement that gives it; giving a name again replaces it from that point on.

Statement Effect
let name = expr Names any value: number, field, distribution, text, pattern, list. Every ~ in expr is drawn now, once.
let name(params) = expr Defines a function. See Your own functions.
field name = expr Like let, but the value must be a number, a field or a pattern (not a text or a distribution).
pattern name = repeat N event(attrs) Makes a pattern of N events. See Patterns.
constraint expr The edition is valid only if expr is true (not 0). If not, the whole edition is drawn again. expr must be a fixed value.
render kind(args) Produces a file. kind is image, sound, video or sculpture. See Renders.
output expr What the work gives when another work calls it. At most one per work; it must be a field or a pattern.
grow over N for S { name = start then next … } Fields that evolve generation by generation on a grid. See Growing.

A work must contain at least one render, unless it's only used as a component (then it needs an output).

Expressions

Precedence

From the loosest to the tightest binding:

Level Operators Associativity
1 or left
2 and left
3 < > <= >= == != left
4 + - left
5 * / % left
6 unary - prefix
7 ^ right
8 ~ ~~ prefix

So -2 ^ 2 is −4, 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 2⁹, and ~normal(0, 1) * 2 draws first and then doubles. Use parentheses when in doubt.

Operators

Operator Meaning
a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b arithmetic, point by point
a % b remainder, always between 0 and b for a positive b
a ^ b a to the power b
< > <= >= == != 1 where true, 0 where false
a and b 1 where both are non-zero
a or b 1 where either is non-zero
-a negation
~d a draw from distribution d (see Chance)
~~d a grain: a draw from d at every point

Operators work on numbers and fields alike: if either side varies over the canvas, so does the result. A division by zero gives an infinite or undefined value, which renders as 0.

Calls

name(args) calls, in this order of lookup: a work brought in with use, then a primitive, then a distribution, a measure or a function. Primitives and works accept named arguments; functions, distributions and measures take unnamed ones only.

Choices

choose { 3: a | 2: b | 1: c }
choose { a | b | c }

Picks one branch at random, in proportion to its weight (1 when omitted), and evaluates only that branch. Weights must be fixed, zero or positive numbers, not all zero. A branch can give any kind of value.

Values

Kind Examples Where it can be used
number 3, ~between(0, 1), pi anywhere a field is expected, and wherever a fixed value is required
field x, sin(x * 10), circle() arithmetic, functions, primitives, renders
pattern repeat 50 event(…), scatter() as a field (each event a soft spot), in count, as the second argument of sound / video
distribution normal(0, 1) only behind ~ or ~~, or named with let
text "night" render options (palette, format…), text, picture, font, channel, axis, parameters, choose
list [1, 2, 3], [0.3, 0.5] (a point) indexing, loops, arithmetic (element by element), list functions, merge, path…
function let f(a) = … calls only
painting paint(f, palette: "sea") mosaic, place, overlay, render image, render video, output (not arithmetic)
sound drone(f), notes(p), texture(f) render sound, a video's sound:

A number is a field that is the same everywhere. A fixed value is a number that doesn't depend on x, y, t or a grain. Fixed values are required by: distribution parameters, choose weights, constraints, a pattern's count and event attributes, render options, clouds(detail:) and scatter(count:, size:).

Chance

Distributions

Distribution Parameters Gives
uniform(a, b) any a, b a value from a to b, all equally likely
between(a, b) same as uniform
normal(m, d) d > 0 values around m, with spread d (about 68 % within d)
around(m, d) same as normal
beta(a, b) a > 0, b > 0 a value from 0 to 1; average a / (a + b)
poisson(λ) λ > 0 a whole number, average λ
exponential(λ) λ > 0 a positive value, average 1 / λ

A distribution is a value of its own: let d = normal(0, 1), then ~d.

When draws happen

~d draws one number at the moment its expression is evaluated:

Written in Drawn
a let, field, constraint, render or output once per edition
a pattern's event attributes once per event
the count of repeat once per edition
a work parameter's default once per call of that work
a choose branch only if that branch is chosen
a primitive's omitted parameter once per call of that primitive

A name bound with let keeps its value: let r = ~d used twice is the same number twice; ~d written twice is two numbers.

~~d gives a grain: a field whose value at each point (x, y, t) is a separate draw from d. It changes from point to point and from frame to frame, but is fixed by the edition's seed.

Primitives

Shared conventions:

  • Positions and sizes are fractions of the canvas: x, y from 0 to 1, from the top-left; size: 0.5 is half the canvas width.
  • Angles are in degrees; positive angles turn clockwise.
  • Shapes are 1 inside and 0 outside. Textures range from 0 to 1.
  • An omitted parameter is decided by alea, as shown in the tables: a range means a fresh random value for each call; a single value is a fixed default. Except for clouds(detail:) and scatter, every parameter can itself be a field, for example size: 0.2 + 0.1 * t.
  • Arguments can be given in the order listed, or by name.
  • softness on shapes is the width of the edge, in canvas units.

Shapes

Primitive (parameters in order) Omitted
circle(x, y, size, softness) — size is the diameter x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.15–0.45 · softness 0.003
ring(x, y, size, width, softness) — size is the diameter, width the line x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.2–0.6 · width 0.02 · softness 0.003
rect(x, y, width, height, angle, softness) — centred on x, y x, y 0.25–0.75 · width, height 0.15–0.45 · angle 0–90 · softness 0.003
square(x, y, size, angle, softness) x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.15–0.4 · angle 0–90 · softness 0.003
line(x1, y1, x2, y2, width, softness) — a segment ends 0.1–0.9 · width 0.01 · softness 0.002
blob(x, y, size, wobble, softness) — an irregular round shape; wobble from 0 (a circle) up x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.2–0.45 · wobble 0.35 · softness 0.003

Textures

Primitive Omitted
stripes(count, angle, softness) — count stripes across; angle 0 gives vertical stripes, 90 horizontal; softness from 0 (sharp) to 1 (smooth) count 4–16 (whole) · angle 0–180 · softness 0.3
waves(count, angle, height, wiggles, softness) — wavy stripes; height of the waves, wiggles along each stripe count 4–12 · angle 0–180 · height 0.01–0.04 · wiggles 1–5 · softness 0.3
ripples(x, y, count, softness) — rings around x, y x, y 0.25–0.75 · count 5–20 · softness 0.3
dots(count, size, softness) — a grid of count × count dots; size relative to a cell count 5–15 · size 0.5 · softness 0.03
checker(count) — a count × count checkerboard count 4–12
gradient(angle) — 0 to 1 across the canvas; angle 0 goes left to right angle 0–360
glow(x, y, size) — a soft light, brightest at x, y x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.2–0.6
clouds(scale, detail) — smooth noise; scale features across, detail layers (whole, 1–8, fixed) scale 2–6 · detail 4
grain(amount) — random at every point, 0 to amount amount 1
scatter(count, size) — a pattern of random specks (fixed values); each speck's size varies from 0.5 to 1.5 times size count 20–80 · size 0.012

Transforms

The first argument is what is transformed: any shape, texture, picture, pattern or field.

Primitive Omitted
move(shape, x, y) — shifts by x, y x, y −0.25–0.25
rotate(shape, angle, x, y) — turns around x, y angle 0–360 · x, y 0.5
zoom(shape, by, x, y) — scales around x, y; by: 2 is twice as big by 0.5–2 · x, y 0.5
tile(shape, count) — the whole canvas repeated count × count times count 2–6
mirror(shape, axis) — adds the reflection across the vertical centre line ("vertical"), the horizontal one ("horizontal"), or both ("both") axis "vertical"
kaleidoscope(shape, sides, x, y) — repeats the wedge to the right of x, y all around it, mirrored, sides times sides 3–12 · x, y 0.5
warp(shape, amount, scale) — bends space; amount is how far points move, scale how many bends across amount 0.02–0.08 · scale 2–5

Combining

Primitive Gives
merge(a, b, …) the highest value at each point: everything (two or more arguments)
overlap(a, b, …) the lowest value at each point: only where all are (two or more)
cut(shape, by) shape with by removed: shape × (1 − by)
invert(shape) 1 − shape
threshold(shape, level, softness) — a crisp edge where shape crosses level level 0.5 · softness 0.02

Also: mix(a, b, amount) in Functions, and plain arithmetic.

Your own content

These two default to readable: level text, a picture filling the width.

Primitive Omitted
text(words, x, y, size, angle, font, align) — one line of text at x, y; size is the line's height x, y 0.25–0.75 · size 0.06–0.15 · angle 0 · font "sans" · align "center"
picture(file, x, y, size, angle, channel) — an image centred on x, y; size is its width, the height follows its proportions x, y 0.5 · size 1 · angle 0 · channel "luminance"
  • words and file are required texts. Text is a single line.
  • font: "sans", "bold", "serif", "mono" (built in), or the path to a .ttf / .otf file (Japanese, say: see exhibition/fonts/).
  • align: where x, y is on the line: "center" (the middle), "left" (its start: lines of a paragraph, one under the other) or "right" (its end).
  • picture reads PNG, JPEG and WebP; larger than 4096 pixels, it is scaled down. channel: "luminance" (brightness), "red", "green", "blue", or "alpha" (transparency, to use a cut-out as a shape). Transparent areas count as 0.
  • Outside the text's or picture's rectangle, the value is 0.

Functions

All take unnamed arguments and work on numbers and fields.

Function Gives
sin(a) cos(a) tan(a) trigonometry, a in radians (tau is a full turn)
abs(a) sign(a) absolute value; −1, 0 or 1
sqrt(a) exp(a) ln(a) square root, eᵃ, natural logarithm
floor(a) fract(a) rounded down; what is after the decimal point (a − floor(a))
min(a, b) max(a, b) the smaller, the larger
atan2(y, x) the angle of the direction (x, y), in radians
step(edge, a) 1 where a ≥ edge, else 0
clamp(a, lo, hi) a kept between lo and hi
mix(a, b, amount) a + (b − a) × amount
smoothstep(e0, e1, a) 0 below e0, 1 above e1, a smooth curve between
distance(x1, y1, x2, y2) the distance between two points; distance(x, y, 0.5, 0.5) is the distance to the centre
noise(x, y, z) smooth noise between −1 and 1, different for each edition; vary z (for example with t) to animate it

Measures

Fixed values computed from a whole field, for constraints (and anywhere a number is needed):

Measure Gives
mean(f) the average value
stddev(f) how much the values vary
minimum(f), maximum(f) the lowest and highest values
count(p) the number of events of pattern p

mean, stddev, minimum and maximum sample the field on a 24 × 24 grid at four moments (t = 0, ⅓, ⅔, 1).

Lists

Written Gives
[a, b, c] a list (any values, lists included; a trailing comma is allowed)
[expr for name in list] a list with expr computed for each element, bound to name
[expr for a in l1 for b in l2] loops inside loops (the last one changes fastest)
list[i] element i: 0 is the first, −1 the last; i must be a fixed whole number inside the list
point.x, point.y point[0], point[1]

A point is a list of two values, [x, y]. In a loop, each ~ is drawn again for every element, in order. Lists hold at most 100 000 elements.

Arithmetic (+ - * / % ^, comparisons, and, or, unary -) and the functions work element by element: two lists must have the same length; a single value applies to every element. mix(a, b, 0.5) on two points is the point halfway between them.

Function Gives
range(n), range(a, b) the whole numbers 0 … n − 1, or a … b − 1
count(list) the number of elements
sum(list), mean(list), minimum(list), maximum(list) over the elements (numbers or fields); stddev(list) too
merge(list), overlap(list) of all the shapes in the list
join(a, b, …) the lists end to end (a value that is not a list joins as one element)
slice(list, from, to) elements from to to − 1; negative positions count from the end
reverse(list) the same elements, last first
distance(p, q) the distance between two points
path(points, width, softness) the line through the points (at least 2), with round joints; width 0.01 · softness 0.002
length(points) the length of that line
along(points, d) the point at distance d along it, from the start (clamped to the ends)

Your own functions

let snap(v, step = 24) = floor(v * step + 0.5) / step
  • The body is one expression, computed at each call. Each ~ in it is drawn at each call.
  • A function sees the names given before its definition, and its own parameters; not the names given after it, and not itself (so it can't call itself).
  • Arguments are given in order or by name, like a primitive's. A parameter with a default can be left out; the default is computed at each call and can use the parameters before it.
  • A function is called before anything else of the same name (a work brought in with use, a primitive, a function of the language).

Patterns

pattern name = repeat count event(x: …, y: …, t: …, intensity: …, size: …)
  • count is a fixed whole number from 0 to 100 000 (it can be drawn: repeat ~poisson(60)).
  • The attributes are evaluated once per event, so each ~ in them is drawn again for every event. They must be fixed values (not depend on x, y, t or a grain).
  • Inside the attributes, i is the event's index (0 to n − 1) and n the number of events.
  • All attributes are optional:
Attribute Meaning Omitted
x, y position uniform from 0 to 1
t moment, from 0 to 1 uniform from 0 to 1
intensity strength 1
size spread of the event's spot (and length of its note) 0.02

As a field, a pattern is the sum of one soft round spot per event: intensity at its centre, fading over a radius of about 2 × size.

In a sound (second argument of sound or video), each event is a bell-like note: see sound.

Growing

grow over 160 for 360 {
  cells = ~~uniform(0, 1) < 0.3
    then neighbours(cells) == 3 or (cells and neighbours(cells) == 2)
  trace = 0
    then max(trace * 0.95, cells)
}
Part Meaning Omitted
over N the grid has N × N cells over the unit square; whole, 4–1024, fixed 128
for S the number of generations after the first; whole, 1–100 000, fixed 200
name = start then next one grown field (at least one line; names distinct)

How it runs. When the edition is drawn, every start is computed at the centre of every cell (t = 0): that is generation 0. Then, S times, every next is computed at every cell from the previous generation: inside next, each grown name (its own and the other lines') means the previous generation. t inside next is the moment of the generation being left, g / S. A ~ in a rule is drawn once; a ~~ gives each cell, at each generation, its own draw. Values that are not finite become 0. In start, the block's own names still mean what they meant before the block, if anything.

Afterwards, each name is a field of x, y and t: t = 0 is the first generation and t = 1 the last. Between cells the values are blended (bilinearly), between generations too (linearly), and the grid wraps around on all sides (a torus): the canvas outside the unit square repeats it.

Neighbourhood functions, only inside next, on any field (usually a grown name), measured in cells of this grid:

Function Gives
neighbours(f) (or neighbors) the sum of f over the 8 surrounding cells
spread(f) the discrete Laplacian: 0.2 × each side cell + 0.05 × each corner − the cell itself; adding it diffuses f
nearby(f, r) the average of f over the cells within r cells (a disc, the cell included); r whole, 1–12, fixed

Kept generations. At most 600 generations are kept, evenly spaced, and no more than about 64 million values in all (cells × fields × generations kept); the others are computed but not kept, so a video moves through the kept ones. Rules that don't change the work (a chemistry map, a mask) are computed once, not at every generation.

Paintings

A painting is a field in colour, or paintings laid out. Images and videos show it in its own colours; it is computed as pixels, each part at the size it occupies on the canvas.

Function Parameters (in order) Gives
paint field, palette ("ink", or a list of colours), range (measured), alpha (1), bands (0) the field through the palette. range: [low, high] maps those values to the ends of the palette; without it, the range is measured once over the whole animation (ignoring the extreme 0.5 % at each end). alpha is a field, 0 (transparent) to 1
mosaic paintings (a list), columns (√n, rounded up), gap (0.01), background (0) a grid filling the canvas: cells of equal size, row after row, gap apart (a fraction of the canvas's shorter side). Each cell shows a whole painting as a canvas of its own. background is a grey level (0–1) or a painting
place painting, x (0.5), y (0.5), width (0.5), height (= width) the painting in that rectangle (centred on x, y, in canvas units), transparent elsewhere
overlay paintings (any number, or a list), then blend ("normal"), opacity (1), mask (1) the first painting, then each next one over it. blend: normal, add, screen, multiply, lighten, darken, difference, overlay. opacity (0–1) and the mask field (0–1) say how much of each upper layer shows

A field given where a painting is expected is painted in "ink". Where a painting is transparent all the way down, the image is black. A work's output can be a painting. A video of a painting has no sound unless it is given sound: layers.

Time and filters

Functions that take time use t when it is not given.

Function Parameters (in order) Gives
progress start, end, time (t) clamp((time − start) / (end − start), 0, 1)
ease value, kind ("in-out") the value clamped to 0–1, through a curve: linear, in (cubic), out (cubic), in-out (smoothstep), sine, back (overshoots by about 10 %), elastic, bounce. On a list, each element
keys frames (a list of [time, value], times fixed and in order), ease ("linear"), time (t) the first value before the first time, the last after the last, eased between each pair. Values can be numbers, fields or lists of the same shape (points)
sequence items (fields or paintings), fade (0.1), time (t) item i shows from i/n to (i+1)/n, crossfading over fade around each change (at most 1/n). If any item is a painting, a painting
at of (a field or a painting), time the field or painting evaluated with time in place of t, everywhere inside it
lfo times (1), shape ("sine"), phase (0, in turns), from (0), to (1), time (t) with u = fract(time × times + phase): sine 0.5 − 0.5 cos(2π(time × times + phase)); triangle 1 − abs(2u − 1); saw u; square step(0.5, u); pulse (1 − u)⁴; then scaled from from to to. A whole number of times loops over the work
orbit radius (0.25, or [rx, ry]), times (1, or [tx, ty]), phase (0, in turns), x (0.5), y (0.5), time (t) the point [x + rx cos(2π(time × tx + phase)), y + ry sin(2π(time × ty + phase))]: clockwise on the canvas (y grows downwards)

Field filters give a field:

Function Parameters Gives
blur of, radius (0.01) a Gaussian average over 40 points on a spiral, out to twice the radius
pixelate of, size (0.02) the value at the centre of each square cell
edges of, step (0.002) the length of the difference across ±step, in x and y
relief of, angle (135), depth (10), step (0.003) 0.5 + depth × (f towards the light − f away from it)
posterize of, levels (6) floor(clamp(f, 0, 1) × levels) / (levels − 1)
film of, amount (0.08) f + amount × a uniform grain in [−1, 1], different at every point and frame
vignette of, amount (0.5) f × (1 − amount × smoothstep(0.25, 0.75, distance to the centre))

Painting filters give a painting; they work on the pixels, at the size the painting is drawn:

Function Parameters Gives
blur of, radius (0.01, up to 0.3) a separable Gaussian of that spread, as a fraction of the shorter side
pixelate of, size (0.02) the average of each square block
film of, amount (0.08) grain on each channel, new at every frame
vignette of, amount (0.5) darker towards the corners
bloom of, amount (0.8, up to 4) what is brighter than about half, blurred near and far, screened back on
chroma of, amount (0.5, up to 4) red pushed outwards and blue inwards from the centre, by 2 % × amount of the distance

bloom and chroma given a field paint it in "ink" first; edges, relief and posterize need a field.

Inputs

Files

Function Gives
open(file) the file, read as an input (below): an image, a sound, a MIDI file or a text, recognised by its contents. file is a text, a path from the work's folder
files(pattern) a list of texts: the files whose names match, as paths from the work's folder (ready for open), in order of name. * stands for any run of characters, ? for one, in the file name only ("photos/*.jpg", not "*/a.jpg"); names starting with . are left out. No match is an error
choose(list) one element of the list, all equally likely: one draw, the same as choose { list[0] \| list[1] \| … }

open and files reach the work's folder and the folders inside it, never further (no absolute path, no ..), so a work and its files can travel together, and a web page made with --web carries them (every file files lists is bundled). Opening a file makes no draw; each file is read once per run, and shown with the edition, by name and fingerprint.

What comes in

input(name, or) gives what the work was given: the default input (name omitted) comes from the pipe or --in FILE; a named one from --in NAME=FILE. Without one, or is used: a text is a file to read (relative to the work), anything else is used as it is. Without either, an error. or is computed in every case, so the work makes the same draws with or without an input.

An input is recognised by its first bytes: PNG, JPEG or WebP (an image), WAV (a sound: PCM 8, 16, 24 or 32 bits, or float, at most two channels and ten minutes), a Standard MIDI File (format 0 or 1, in ticks per quarter note), otherwise UTF-8 text. Inputs make no draw.

Image Gives
.luma (.luminance), .red, .green, .blue, .alpha, .hue, .saturation, .lightness a field, 0 to 1 (transparent pixels give 0; hue goes round from red at 0). The image is centred and covers the canvas: its shorter side spans 0 to 1
.painting the image in its own colours, placed the same way
.width, .height, .aspect its size in pixels, and height ÷ width
colours(image, count) (5) a list of count colours (1–32), "#rrggbb", darkest first: k-means on up to 16 000 of its pixels, always the same for the same image

An image input sets the default size of images (its own size) and the proportions of videos (width 720 and the image's proportions).

Sound Gives
.level the loudness along the sound (t = 0 at its start, 1 at its end), 200 values per second, scaled so the loudest 1 % reach 1; quick to rise, slower to fall
.bass, .mid, .treble the same through a band: 20–200, 200–2000, 2000–16 000 Hz (fourth-order filters)
band(sound, low, high) the same for any band, in Hz
.pulse each beat: its strength, then an exponential fade (0.18 s)
.beats a pattern: one event per onset (a sudden rise in three bands, at least 0.1 s apart), at the time of the onset; intensity its strength (0.2–1); position drawn from the edition's seed (no draw is made)
.duration seconds
sound: [song], render sound(song) the sound itself, as a layer: not through the room or the echo

A sound input sets the default duration of videos and sounds (its own, at most 600 s).

Text Gives
.text all of it
.words, .lines lists of texts (blank lines skipped)
.rows a list per line: cells split on , ; or tabs (otherwise spaces); a cell that reads as a number is a number
MIDI file Gives
.notes a pattern: one event per note of every track, in time order. t and x are its start over the file (0 to 1), y its pitch over the file's range (the lowest note at the bottom, the highest at the top), intensity its velocity ÷ 127, size 0.006 + 0.004 × its length in seconds (at most 2)
.tracks a list of patterns, one per track that has notes (the same heights as .notes)
.names the tracks' names (or track N)
.tempo the file's first tempo, in beats per minute (120 without one)
.duration seconds, until the last note ends
.level how much is sounding along the file: the velocities of the notes held, each fading over 0.05 s after it ends, scaled so the loudest 1 % reach 1

A note read from a MIDI file keeps its pitch and its length: a notes layer plays it as written, whatever its height, scale, key or harmony (an arp takes only its rhythm), and render midi writes it back as it was (a drum on channel 10 stays the same drum). Tempo changes anywhere in the file are followed. A MIDI file sets the default duration of videos and sounds, as a sound does.

A default given as a value stands in for the input: its channels and curves (.luma, .level…) are itself, .alpha is 1, .painting paints it in "ink", and colours gives "ink" colours.

Music: meters, rhythms, harmony

Function Parameters (in order) Gives
meter tempo (120; 20–400), bars (8), beats (4) a meter: .length = bars × beats × 60 ÷ tempo seconds (at most 600), .tempo, .bars, .beats, .bar, .beat (seconds)
euclid hits, steps (1–64), rotate (0), bars (1, or a meter), y (0.5) a pattern: in each bar, a hit on step k when ((k − rotate) × hits) mod steps < hits; t = x = the step's moment over the work; intensity 1 on the first hit of the cycle, 0.8 otherwise
steps pattern (a text, or a number of steps 1–64), bars (1, or a meter), y (0.5), density (0.5) a written pattern: X 1, x 0.65, o 0.35, . - _ rest, spaces ignored, \| the next bar (the bars written repeat over bars). A number: a hit on each step with the probability of the field at (t, 0.5, t), clamped to 0–1 (intensity 0.5 + 0.5 × it); drawn from the edition's seed without a draw
chords progression (a text), key ("A3", 220 Hz), scale ("major"; any scale of semitones), bars (4, or a meter: its tempo goes with the progression), tension (0.4), repeat (1) a progression over the work. Written: chords separated by spaces, , or \|, each with an optional :weight, repeated repeat times, sharing the time by weight. "functional": bars chords, see below
arp harmony, rhythm (a pattern), mode ("up"), octaves (2; 1–5), gate (0.8), instrument ("pluck"), key (the progression's), gain (1), tempo (the progression's meter), swing (0.5), humanize (0) a notes layer: the r-th event in time order plays step r of the mode over the chord's tones, ascending over octaves octaves from the key's register; held gate × the time to the next event (in MIDI)

Roman numerals are counted on the scale (a scale of other than seven notes uses the major or minor scale it is closest to): I–VII, upper case major (0 4 7), lower case minor (0 3 7), then ° (0 3 6; °7 adds 9), ø (0 3 6 10), + (0 4 8), 7 (adds 10), maj7 (11), 9 (10 and 14), 6 (9), sus2/sus4 (the third becomes 2 or 5); b/# before the numeral lower or raise the root. Chord names: a letter A–G, # or b, then nothing (major), m, dim, aug, 7, maj7, m7, m7b5, dim7, sus2, sus4, 6, m6, 9, m9 or add9; their roots are counted from the key's note.

"functional": chord 1 is I and the last is I, with V before it; the others walk between functions, tonic (I 0.5, vi 0.35, iii 0.15), subdominant (IV 0.55, ii 0.45) and dominant (V 0.8, vii 0.2), from tonic to tonic 0.15, subdominant 0.5, dominant 0.35 + 0.2 × tension; from subdominant to itself 0.15, dominant 0.6 + 0.2 × tension, tonic 0.25; from dominant to tonic 0.8, itself 0.1 + 0.1 × tension, subdominant 0.1. The fourth chord of each phrase is V with probability 0.6 (a half cadence). Chords are the scale's own triads, with its seventh with probability tension × 0.8 for V, tension × 0.35 otherwise; in a minor scale V is made major with probability 0.5 + 0.5 × tension. The draws use the edition's randomness.

A progression's members: .names (a list of texts), .count, .key (Hz), .index (a field of t: 0, 1, 2… which chord is playing).

harmony: on drone: each voice starts on a tone of the first chord (stacked upwards from the layer's key) and, at each change, moves to the nearest pitch of the new chord that no other voice holds, gliding over 60 ms; the default key is the progression's, an octave down. On notes: the height of an event picks among the chord's tones over three octaves from the layer's key (default: the progression's), the bottom of the canvas the lowest. The progression gives the notes, the layer's key the register (the key's pitch class is replaced by the progression's).

swing (0.5–0.75) and humanize (0–1) on notes and arp: on the tempo's grid, every odd sixteenth moves by (swing − 0.5) × 2 sixteenths; humanize moves each note by up to ± 30 ms × humanize and scales its velocity by up to ± 40 % × humanize, from the edition's seed.

Renders

render kind(args) writes one file. A work can have any number of renders; all belong to the same edition. Files are named <work>-<seed>.<ext>, with -1, -2… added when a work has several renders of the same kind.

How values become media. Before being turned into colour, loudness or height, values are stretched to the range they take in that render, ignoring the most extreme 0.5 % at each end (for colour, range: [low, high] sets the range instead). A field that is the same everywhere is shown as it is (0 blank, 1 full).

Canvas shape. When width and height differ, the 0–1 square stays fully visible and centred; the longer side shows more around it.

Options must be fixed values (texts for palette, format, audio).

image

render image(field, …) → PNG

Option Default Range
width 1024 16–8192 pixels
height = width 16–8192 pixels
at 0 the moment t to show
palette "ink" a name or a list of colours: see Palettes
bands, range see Palettes

sound

render sound(layer, layer, …) → WAV, stereo, 44.1 kHz

The layers are sounds made by drone, notes and texture (or lists of them); they are mixed, sent through an echo and a room, and mastered.

Option Default Range
duration 20 0.5–600 seconds
room 0.25 0–1: the size of the space around the sound (0: none; 0.5: a hall, about a second of tail; 0.9: a cathedral)
echo 0 0–1: a ping-pong echo, three eighths of a beat (of the notes' tempo, or 0.375 s)

key can always be a note name ("A3", "C#4", "Bb2"; A4 = 440 Hz) as well as a frequency. With harmony:, see Music above.

drone(field, voices, instrument, scale, key, gain, harmony): voices that hold notes of a scale. Voice k (from 0) listens to the field along the line y = (k + 0.5) / voices, at x = 0.3 and at x = 0.7, as t goes from 0 to 1: it is loud where the field is high there, sounds towards the side where it is higher, and its upper partials open as it gets louder. Voice k plays degree k of the scale (every other degree for scales of six notes or more, so the voices make chords); the first voice, at the top of the canvas, is the lowest.

Parameter Default Values
voices 6 1–24
instrument "sine" "sine", "organ", "reed", "strings" (three players, vibrato), "choir" (a vowel that opens with the field), "glass", "wind" (breath, tuned), or a synth (see Synths below)
scale "pentatonic" see below
key 110 20–2000 Hz: the first note
gain 1 0–10

notes(pattern, instrument, scale, key, gain, tempo, harmony, swing, humanize): each event plays one note. It starts at t × duration (on the nearest sixteenth note if tempo is given, in beats per minute); its y picks the note, over three octaves of the scale from the bottom of the canvas to the top; its x places it between left and right; it rings for about 0.08 + 20 × size seconds (at most 3, longer for bells and glass, shorter for wood and ticks); intensity sets its loudness.

Parameter Default Values
instrument "bell" "bell", "pluck" (a string), "marimba", "kalimba", "glass", "wood", "drum" (two octaves down), "tick", or a synth (see Synths below)
scale "pentatonic" see below
key 220 20–4000 Hz
gain 1 0–10
tempo 0 (free) 0–400 beats per minute

texture(field, kind, gain): an ambience. Its loudness follows the average of the field over the canvas as t runs (stretched to the range it takes).

Parameter Default Values
kind "wind" "wind" (brighter when louder), "waves" (slow swells, out of step between the ears), "rain" (drops, more of them), "crackle" (sparse pops)
gain 1 0–10

Synths: an instrument of your own, built from oscillators, envelopes, filters and effects, and played once per note. synth { … } is a few lets, then one expression: the sound.

let pad = synth {
  let env = adsr(attack: 1.5, decay: 0.5, sustain: 0.8, release: 2)
  let osc = saw() + saw(note.freq * ~around(1.0, 0.003))   // two saws, detuned by chance
  lowpass(osc, cutoff: 300 + 2200 * note.level, resonance: 0.3) * env
}
notes(melody, instrument: pad)      // `drone` and `arp` take a synth the same way

Inside a synth, note is the note being played:

Value What it is
note.freq its frequency, in Hz (the default of every oscillator)
note.velocity how hard it is played, 0–1, from the event's intensity
note.gate 1 while the note is held, then 0
note.time seconds since the note started
