note.level in a drone, how loud the field is there (0–1); 1 for notes

and these names are units (outside a synth, square is still a shape):

Unit Parameters (default) What it does
sine, saw, square, triangle freq (note.freq) an oscillator, from −1 to 1; saw and square are band-limited (no whistling at high notes)
pulse freq (note.freq), width (0.25) a square with its high part width of a cycle long
noise white noise
adsr attack (0.01), decay (0.2), sustain (0.7), release (0.3) an envelope, 0–1: up in attack seconds, down to sustain in decay, held while the note is, then down to 0 in release
perc attack (0.005), release (1) a struck envelope: up in attack, down to silence in release, however long the note
lowpass, highpass, bandpass input, cutoff (1000 Hz), resonance (0.2; 0–1) a resonant filter (state-variable, stable at any setting)
delay input, time (0.3 s), feedback (0.4; 0–0.95), mix (0.35) an echo
drive input, amount (0.5; 0–1) saturation, from warm to fuzzy
chorus input, depth (0.5), rate (0.8 Hz), mix (0.5) a slightly late, swaying copy: width and shimmer

Signals combine with + - * / and numbers; any parameter that is a signal can move (a filter's cutoff following an envelope, an oscillator's frequency bent by another: FM). Envelope times and the delay's and chorus's settings are fixed for the synth: numbers, or ~ draws. A ~ draw in a synth is drawn once per edition, like anywhere else, so each edition has its own timbre. An oscillator at a low frequency is an LFO: sine(5) sways five times a second.

A note sounds for as long as it is held (an arpeggio's gate, or the event's ringing time) plus its adsr release and the tail of its echoes; with only perc envelopes, for as long as they ring. Its loudness already follows the event's intensity, and a drone's the field: note.velocity and note.level are there to shape the timbre too. Each voice ends with a gentle high-pass at 15 Hz, which takes out rumble and any offset from zero. In MIDI files and in the plugin, a synth is named after its let: notes - pad.

Scales: "pentatonic", "minor-pentatonic", "major", "minor", "dorian", "phrygian", "lydian", "mixolydian", "harmonic-minor", "whole-tone", "blues", "hirajoshi", "chromatic" (equal temperament), and "harmonics" (the first eight partials of the key, then the same an octave up).

Each layer is brought to a comparable level before its gain applies; the mix is normalized, gently limited, and faded in and out over half a second.

The original form, render sound(field, pattern, fundamental:, voices:), still works and sounds as before (mono): a sine drone on a five-note scale (1, 9/8, 5/4, 3/2, 5/3 of fundamental, 110 Hz by default) listening at x = 0.5, and bell notes whose pitch rises from 2 to 16 times the fundamental with y.

video

render video(field, pattern?, …) → MP4 (H.264, with AAC sound) or GIF. Needs ffmpeg on the command line.

Option Default Range
duration 10 0.5–600 seconds
fps 30 1–120 frames per second
width 720 16–3840 (rounded down to even)
height = width 16–3840 (rounded down to even)
palette "ink"
format "mp4" "mp4" or "gif"
audio "on" for mp4, "off" for gif "on" or "off" (a gif can't have sound)
sound the original drone and bells a sound or a list of sounds, as in sound
room, echo as in sound
fundamental, voices as in the original sound when there is no sound:

t goes from 0 at the first frame towards 1 (frame k of N is at t = k / N), so a work built on sin(t * tau) loops seamlessly. Colours use one scale for the whole video, so they don't flicker. The soundtrack is the sound: layers if given, otherwise the original drone and bells of the field and pattern.

sculpture

render sculpture(field, …) → STL (binary), a closed solid, in millimetres

Option Default Range
resolution 160 8–1024 points per side
side 100 width and depth, in mm
relief 0.25 height of the tallest point, as a fraction of side
base 4 thickness of the base, in mm (at least 0.5)
at 0 the moment t to sculpt

Palettes

palette is a name or a list of colours.

Palette Colours
ink paper → grey → ink (high values are dark)
sea deep blue → blue → pale turquoise → foam white
ember black → dark red → orange → pale yellow
lichen dark moss → green → pale green → cream
night black → violet → pink → white
["#fff", "#f5d000", "#d40920"] your own: a gradient through these colours, evenly spread from the lowest value to the highest
[[0, "#fff"], [0.6, "#fff"], [0.6, "#d40920"], [1, "#111"]] colours placed at values from 0 to 1, in order; two colours at the same value make a sharp edge

Colours are written "#rrggbb" or "#rgb". With these options (on image, video and paint):

Option Default Effect
bands 0 (smooth) 2–256: the values are cut into that many flat levels, from the first colour to the last. With as many bands as colours, each colour gets one band
range measured [low, high]: those values are the two ends of the palette, instead of the range the field takes (so range: [0, 1] maps a field's values as they are)

---|---| | ink | paper → grey → ink (high values are dark) | | sea | deep blue → blue → pale turquoise → foam white | | ember | black → dark red → orange → pale yellow | | lichen | dark moss → green → pale green → cream | | night | black → violet → pink → white |

midi

render midi(layers…, duration, tempo) → a Standard MIDI File (format 1, 480 ticks per quarter note)

Option Default Range
duration 20 (or a sound input's) 0.5–600 s
tempo the first notes layer's tempo, else 120 1–400 BPM (the file's grid; the notes keep their moments in seconds)

A first track holds the title, the tempo and 4/4; then one track per layer, on its own channel (1, 2, 3…, skipping 10).

Layer Becomes
drone a General MIDI program (sine → 89, organ → 19, reed → 68, strings → 48, choir → 52, glass → 92, wind → 91); each voice a note (the degree it holds), on when its loudness passes 0.06 (velocity 30 + 97 × √loudness), off below 0.02; controller 11 (expression) follows the loudest voice, 25 times a second
notes a program (bell → 14, pluck → 24, marimba → 12, kalimba → 108, glass → 9, wood → 115); a note per event at its moment (on the tempo's grid if it has one), velocity 127 × intensity, held 90 % of its ring. drum and tick go to channel 10, the degree picking from the kit (36 kick, 41, 38 snare, 39, 45, 42 closed hat, 46 open hat, 48, 51 ride, 49 crash) or from ticks (37, 42, 75, 76, 77, 44)
cc(field, number, channel) controller number (74; 0–127) on channel (1; 1–16): the field's mean over the canvas, clamped to 0–1, as 0–127, 50 times a second when it changes. Silent in a sound
texture, a sound input nothing (they have no notes)

Notes are the nearest MIDI notes to alea's pitches. For a scale of semitones whose key falls between two notes, a pitch bend on the channel (range ±2) puts the whole layer in tune; the harmonic series is rounded.

Live MIDI

--midi plays the edition's render midi (else its first render sound of layers, else its first video sound:) in real time, then stops; --loop goes on with new editions (S, S+1… with --seed S), each prepared while the one before plays. --sync waits for a DAW's start and follows its clock (24 ticks per beat): the music's beats at the DAW's tempo, its stop silences the notes, a new start begins the edition again, and with --loop each edition starts on the next bar. Ctrl-C, or the end, sends a note-off for every note still on and "all notes off" (controller 123) on every channel used. Needs the feature midi (except --midi-port print).

Components

A work becomes a component when it has an output; another work brings it in with use and calls it by name.

work Flower(cx = ~between(0.2, 0.8), size = 0.2, petals) { … output … }
  • Parameters are names, optionally with a default. A default is evaluated for each call that doesn't give the parameter, and can use the parameters before it. A parameter without a default must be given by every caller, and makes the work unable to run on its own.
  • A call Flower(…) takes arguments like a primitive (in order, or by name) and returns the work's output. It can be used anywhere a field is.
  • Every call is a new draw. Its seed is drawn from the caller's, so the whole composition replays from one seed. Each instance has its own grain and noise; a field passed in as an argument keeps the caller's.
  • The component's constraints are retried locally: only the component is drawn again.
  • Its renders are ignored when it is called.
  • Its names are its own: a component sees only its parameters and its own statements, not the caller's names.

use

use "lib/flower.alea"
  • Paths are relative to the file containing the use.
  • A file only sees the works it uses itself.
  • Two works with the same name, or a work with the same name as the file's own, is an error. So is a circular use (a uses b, which uses a).

Command line

alea <file.alea> [options]
cat input | alea <file.alea> [options] > output
Option Effect
-s, --seed N draw edition N (decimal or 0x… hexadecimal) instead of a random one
-n, --editions N draw N editions; with --seed S, editions S, S+1, …
-o, --out DIR write files into DIR (default: the current folder). -o -: the first render to the standard output
--in FILE the default input, instead of the pipe; --in - waits for the pipe however long it takes (otherwise, a pipe silent for 3 seconds counts as no input)
--in NAME=FILE a named input, for input("NAME")
--seed-from-input the seed is the input's fingerprint: the same input, the same edition
--midi play the music live on a new virtual MIDI port, "alea"
--midi-port P play to the existing port whose name contains P; print writes the messages as text
--midi-ports list the MIDI ports
--loop with --midi: a new edition after each one, until Ctrl-C
--sync, --sync-port P with --midi: follow a DAW's MIDI clock, from a new port "alea clock" or from P
--check check the work and draw it once (seed 0 unless -s), without writing files
--web FILE write a web page that draws a new edition on every visit
-h, --help show this list

Each edition prints its seed, the fingerprint of each input it read, and the files it wrote. The pipe is read only when the work asks for its input. When the standard output is not a terminal and no -o is given, the first render goes to it and the messages to the error output, so works chain: cat a.png | alea blur.alea | alea frame.alea > b.png. Errors are printed with the file, line and column, and a mark under the problem.

In the browser

  • web/dist/playground.html is the playground: an editor, the examples and the tour, and every render previewed in the page. It is one file and works offline.
  • alea work.alea --web page.html writes a page for one work. A visit draws a random edition; an address ending in #0x… opens that edition.

Both run the same engine as the command line, compiled to WebAssembly, and compute the same images, sounds and sculptures. Videos are previewed in the browser; the MP4 file comes from the command line.

Limits

Limit Value
attempts to satisfy the constraints 1000 per edition (per component)
works nested inside works 16 levels
events in a pattern 100 000
image size 16–8192 pixels per side
video size 16–3840 pixels per side
sound and video duration 0.5–600 seconds
sculpture resolution 8–1024
picture size scaled down beyond 4096 pixels

Reproducibility

An edition is fully determined by its work's files, its seed and its inputs. The same seed gives byte-identical PNG, WAV and STL files on every operating system and in the browser. MP4 and GIF files are encoded by ffmpeg, whose output can vary between ffmpeg versions; their frames don't.

alea uses its own maths library and its own random samplers for this reason: system maths can differ from one platform to another in the last bit, and a draw must not.
